articles.title: Configure a Durable Queue or Fast Streams for Rate-Limiting HTTP-Based Logistics Webhooks
articles.excerpt: Configure a Durable Queue or Fast Streams for Rate-Limiting HTTP-Based Logistics Webhooks To configure a queue for rate-limiting HTTP-based webhook processing in a logistics renewal workflow, choose a…
articles.body: Configure a Durable Queue or Fast Streams for Rate-Limiting HTTP-Based Logistics Webhooks To configure a queue for rate-limiting HTTP-based webhook processing in a logistics renewal workflow, choose a durable queue when missing a business deadline is worse than adding a few milliseconds of handoff time. Choose a fast stream only when the downstream contract can tolerate replay, retention, and consumer-management work. The queue is not the rate limiter. It is the shock absorber; the worker-side limiter is the clock that protects the webhook destination.

articles.title: Compare Cloud Storage Providers for Direct Browser Uploads — Node.js Retention Rules
articles.excerpt: Property management teams should choose browser-upload storage by its trust boundary and retention controls, not by whether its SDK can mint a presigned URL. For training artifacts, the browser should…
articles.body: Property management teams should choose browser-upload storage by its trust boundary and retention controls, not by whether its SDK can mint a presigned URL. For training artifacts, the browser should receive permission for one object, for a short window, with a server-owned key and a separately enforced retention policy. The storage provider matters after those rules are clear. A useful design has three planes: a Node.js service authorizes an upload, the browser sends bytes directly to object storage, and a worker records completion and applies retention metadata. That separation keeps credentials out of the browser, but it does not make the browser trustworthy. It can still retry, abandon a multipart upload, or send an unexpected content type.

articles.title: Webhook Retry Queue: Delayed Jobs and Idempotency in Node.js
articles.excerpt: Short answer: treat a webhook retry queue as an at-least-once transport, and make the durable business change idempotent with a stable event identity and a database transaction. The deciding constrain…
articles.body: Short answer: treat a webhook retry queue as an at-least-once transport, and make the durable business change idempotent with a stable event identity and a database transaction. The deciding constraint is the gap between doing work and acknowledging it. A worker can commit a change, lose its process before the acknowledgement is recorded, and receive the same job again. No reasonable retry policy can infer whether that first change happened. Delayed jobs help recovery; they do not close that gap. For an AI application, that distinction matters twice. A repeated state change can corrupt customer state, while a repeated call to a model or external API can consume latency and usage budget without producing a new result. Keep the queue simple, but make its boundaries explicit.

articles.title: Never let the model retype a number: how we read lab reports with two AI passes
articles.excerpt: People photograph a blood test report and ask "is this bad?". When we built the lab report explainer in Saluvo, the explanation turned out to be the easy part. The risky part is reading the numbers: a…
articles.body: People photograph a blood test report and ask "is this bad?". When we built the lab report explainer in Saluvo, the explanation turned out to be the easy part. The risky part is reading the numbers: a misplaced decimal turns a normal result into an alarming one, or the reverse. These are the design rules we ended up with. None of them need a special model, and they apply to any LLM pipeline that pulls numbers out of documents: invoices, prescriptions, bank statements. 1. Extraction is copying, not understanding The extraction prompt is deliberately dull: Copy every test row exactly as printed. Never guess a value; skip a row you cannot read. Values come back as strings exactly as printed ( "7.8" , "1,250" , "<0.5" ), at temperature 0, in a strict JSON shape.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

articles.body: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.
